title: Predictive Structure to Thermal Conductivity Modeling Framework for BEOL Interconnect Stacks in Advanced Technology Nodes Enabled by Extensive Layer Resolved Thermal Measurements
authors: Zifeng Huang, Yiyang Sun, Tianyu Jia, Runsheng Wang, Zhe Cheng
abstract: The increasing structural complexity of BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced integrated circuits demands a structure-aware thermal conductivity (\k{appa}) modeling framework. However, generalizable models derived from layer-resolved thermal measurements that quantitatively capture the dependence of \k{appa} on interconnect structures remain lacking, limiting predictive thermal analysis. Here, we establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware \k{appa} modeling framework enabled by time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with ~100 nm depth resolution. Statistical analysis of a compiled dataset comprising over 40 experimentally measured layer-resolved \k{appa} values across diverse BEOL layers reveals a generalizable empirical structure-to-\k{appa} relationship, enabling predictive modeling based on interconnect structure. An intra-layer three-dimensional \k{appa} distribution model based on effective medium theory and realistic layouts further resolves spatial \k{appa} variations within practical interconnect layers. Together, these models establish an experimentally derived, structure-aware \k{appa} modeling framework for predictive and generalizable thermal analysis of advanced interconnect stacks and 3D ICs.
summary: This paper develops a novel, structure-aware framework to predict the thermal conductivity of complex BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced microelectronics. By combining extensive time-domain thermoreflectance measurements with statistical modeling, the authors create an empirical model that accounts for nanoscale structural variations. This allows for highly accurate thermal analysis, which is crucial for preventing hotspots in next-generation 3D integrated circuits.
main_problem: The increasing structural complexity of BEOL interconnect stacks in advanced ICs requires a structure-aware thermal conductivity modeling framework because conventional models fail to capture local thermal variations.
main_result: The authors established an experimentally derived, generalizable framework that predicts thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) based on interconnect structure, showing that neglecting local inhomogeneity underestimates temperature rise.
method: The framework combines Time-Domain Thermoreflectance (TDTR) measurements to gather extensive layer-resolved data, which is then used with statistical analysis and Effective Medium Theory (EMT) to build predictive models.
model_or_system: The physical system is the Back-End-of-Line (BEOL) interconnect stack in advanced integrated circuits. The model predicts $\kappa$ as a function of structural parameters like linewidth ($w$) and Cu volume fraction ($f$).
key_observables: Thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), layer-resolved $\kappa$ distributions, and maximum temperature rise.
important_parameters: Interconnect linewidth ($w$), Cu volume fraction ($f$), and thermal boundary resistance (TBR) parameters ($A, B, w_0$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes that the thermal behavior can be generalized from measured layer-resolved data and that EMT can accurately map spatial variations within layers.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the TDTR setup, sample preparation, the empirical $\kappa$ prediction model vs. experimental data, and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) results comparing averaged vs. spatially resolved thermal predictions.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitations of current thermal models (motivation) to presenting the experimental methodology (TDTR measurements on BEOL stacks), deriving the structure-aware empirical model, and finally validating the framework using FEA to demonstrate the necessity of local thermal inhomogeneity.
